prose.summary: An actuary prices risk for a living: what a claim will cost, how long a pension has to last, what a premium needs to be so the company doesn't lose money on the bet it just made. People confuse it with financial analysis, but an analyst reads markets that already exist; an actuary builds the model that decides what a product should cost before anyone has bought it. The exams are what separate the two, not the math.
prose.day_to_day: Most weeks split between building or updating a model in Excel or Python and defending what that model assumes. You'll open last quarter's reserve file, check it against new claims data, and flag where the assumptions are drifting from reality. There's usually one meeting where you present a number to underwriting or finance and they push back on it, which is the part people either dread or look forward to depending on how the model held up. A chunk of time, often blocked off on the calendar, goes to studying for the next exam, and employers generally protect that block even when deadlines are tight. Report writing eats the rest: memos that explain not just the number but why it's defensible if a regulator asks. The good week is the one where the model clears review with no revisions.
prose.work_environment: This is desk work, almost entirely computer-based, and the 60 percent remote share reflects that the deliverable is a spreadsheet or a report, not a physical presence anywhere. Hours run standard business week most of the year, with predictable spikes around quarter-end reserving and year-end pricing cycles when the models have to close on schedule. On-call is rare; the pressure is calendar-driven, not phone-driven. Offices skew quiet: small teams, a lot of solo modeling time, punctuated by scheduled reviews rather than constant interruption. Travel is minimal unless the role touches client-facing consulting.
prose.getting_in: The credential is the career: SOA or CAS exams, 7 to 10 of them, taken while you work, with most employers funding the materials and giving paid study time. Getting to ASA or ACAS runs 4 to 7 years; fellowship, if you go for it, takes longer. Most postings (8 of them in what's measured here) still ask for a specific degree, usually math, statistics, or actuarial science, though 2 accept adjacent quantitative backgrounds without naming the major. The stall point is almost always exam 2 or 3, where study hours start competing hard with a full-time job and people either find a rhythm or stop progressing. Two years of experience is the median asked for even at entry-adjacent postings, so the first job typically comes with one exam already passed, not zero.
prose.ladder: Early on you own a piece of a model: one line of business, one state's rate filing, one reserve segment. Passing exams unlocks scope before it unlocks title, so the real step up is when you start signing off on numbers instead of just producing them, which usually lines up with reaching ASA or ACAS. After that the ladder forks: chief actuary and management track, where you own relationships with regulators and the board, or fellowship and staying technical, where you go deep on pricing or reserving methodology and let someone else run the meetings. That fork tends to show up 6 to 8 years in, once fellowship is in sight.
prose.suits: People who like this work tend to like the moment a model finally reconciles, when the number you built survives three rounds of scrutiny from underwriting, finance, and a regulator and still holds. It rewards someone who's comfortable being the person who has to defend an assumption out loud, calmly, in a room that wants a different answer. The ones who leave are usually people who wanted the math without the exam treadmill, or who wanted faster feedback than a quarterly reserve cycle gives you. If you like puzzles that get argued over for a week, this fits; if you want to see your work ship in a day, it won't.
prose.misconceptions: The common one is that actuaries just crunch numbers alone all day. In practice a large share of the job is presentation and negotiation: convincing underwriting or the board that your assumption is the right one, which is why presentation and business-development skills show up as often as they do in postings. Another is that the credential is optional polish. It isn't; without it you're capped at analyst-adjacent work no matter how good your models are.
prose.who_qualifies: Underwriters carry the closest match, since they already read risk the way an actuary prices it, just from the other side of the desk. Financial analysts transfer well too: the modeling and Excel fluency carry over directly, though they usually arrive without any exams passed. Economists and market researchers bring the statistical reasoning but tend to be weaker on insurance-specific mechanics like reserving and loss development, which the exams cover. Accountants carry the accounting skill that's the single most-requested skill in postings, but the transition still runs through the exam sequence like everyone else's does.
prose.what_the_numbers_miss: None of this shows what it feels like to fail an exam you studied 200 hours for and have to schedule it again for six months out, which happens to almost everyone at least once. It also doesn't capture how much of the job, at the senior level, is politics: whose assumption wins in a room, not whose math is more correct.

steps.do: Get a degree with heavy math or statistics
steps.how: Most postings still ask for one, and it's the foundation the exams build on. Actuarial science, math, or statistics degrees are most common; a quantitative economics or engineering degree with a strong stats sequence works for the 2 in 10 postings that don't name a specific major. Four years, done before you're job hunting seriously.

steps.do: Pass the first two actuarial exams
steps.how: Probability and financial mathematics are the standard opening pair for SOA or CAS. Most candidates start studying in their last year of school or right after; each exam typically takes 100 to 300 study hours depending on background. You're done with this step once you have an offer letter, since most entry-level roles want at least one exam passed already.

steps.do: Take an entry-level actuarial analyst role
steps.how: Look for insurers, reinsurers, or consultancies that explicitly fund exam study time and materials, since most do. This is where the 2-year median experience figure gets built: you'll rotate through reserving, pricing, or valuation work while continuing to sit exams on the company's clock.

steps.do: Clear the remaining exams toward ASA or ACAS
steps.how: This is the long stretch: 5 to 7 more exams over roughly 3 to 5 years, layered on top of full-time work. You know you're done when the designation letters show up after your name and your employer stops asking when the next exam is.

Once associateship is done, decide whether to keep sitting fellowship exams (2 to 4 more years, deep technical specialization) or move toward leading a team and owning client or regulator relationships instead. Both are viable; the postings that pay toward the $180k mark tend to want one or the other clearly chosen.

prose.tools: Excel is still the daily instrument, non-negotiable, and shows up in nearly half of postings for a reason: reserving and pricing models often live there even after everything else has modernized. Python and SQL are now requested in a third to 40 percent of postings, mostly for data pulls and automating what used to be manual spreadsheet work, and that share is the one moving upward. Statistical and financial modeling knowledge matters more than any specific software; the tool changes, the underlying method doesn't.

industries.name: Life and health insurance
industries.note: Long time horizons: you're pricing products that pay out decades from now, so the work leans on mortality and lapse assumptions more than on quarterly results.

industries.name: Property and casualty insurance
industries.note: Shorter feedback loops than life insurance; claims develop and pay out within a year or two, so you see whether your pricing was right much sooner.

industries.name: Consulting
industries.note: Pension and benefits work for corporate clients, more client-facing and presentation-heavy than in-house roles, with more variety of problems but less depth on any one book of business.

industries.name: Reinsurance
industries.note: Pricing risk for insurers rather than individuals, larger and more volatile numbers, and a smaller, more senior-skewed set of roles.

specializations.name: Predictive modeling / data science for pricing
specializations.why: Insurers are pushing pricing models past traditional actuarial tables into machine-learning territory, and the 40 percent of postings asking for Python signal where hiring is already headed.

specializations.name: Enterprise risk management
specializations.why: Regulatory capital requirements keep expanding, and actuaries who can model risk across an entire company rather than one product line move into chief risk officer tracks faster.

specializations.name: Longevity and pension risk
specializations.why: Aging populations are straining pension funds worldwide, and actuaries who specialize in longevity assumptions are in steady demand from both pension funds and reinsurers picking up that risk.

pros: The moment a reserve estimate finally reconciles with actual claims a year later is a real, specific kind of satisfaction that few finance jobs offer.
Employers pay for your exam study time and materials, so the credential that defines your career costs you very little out of pocket.
The work stays intellectually live for decades because the underlying risks (mortality, climate, interest rates) keep shifting under the models.
60 percent of postings offer remote work, so you can do the core of the job, the modeling and the report writing, from wherever you want.
cons: The exams take years and layer on top of a full-time job, so your 20s or early career involve studying most weekends whether you feel like it or not.
Failing an exam after months of preparation is common and there's no way around retaking it and waiting for the next sitting.
Advancement is gated by the exam sequence itself, so a great year of work doesn't move you up if you haven't cleared the next exam.
The job rewards being right about assumptions that won't be tested for years, which means you rarely get quick confirmation that your work was correct.

faq.q: how long does it take to become an actuary
faq.a: Reaching ASA or ACAS typically takes 4 to 7 years of exams taken alongside full-time work, starting from an entry-level analyst role. Fellowship, if you pursue it, adds more years beyond that; the exams are the timeline, not a fixed number of years of employment.

faq.q: can you become an actuary without a math degree
faq.a: It's harder but not impossible: 8 of the measured postings ask for a specific degree, usually math, statistics, or actuarial science, while 2 accept other quantitative backgrounds. What matters more than the major is whether you can pass the first two exams, which requires the same math regardless of what your diploma says.

faq.q: actuary vs underwriter, what's the difference
faq.a: An underwriter decides whether to accept an individual risk and at what price using rules an actuary already built; an actuary builds the pricing model and the assumptions behind it. Underwriters are the largest single feeder into actuarial roles, with a 55 percent skill match, because the two jobs think about risk the same way from different ends.

faq.q: is being an actuary a good career right now
faq.a: The pay is strong (median $138k, reaching $180k at the 75th percentile) and the switch rate out of the field is low at 2.6 percent a year, which suggests people who get through the exams tend to stay. The tradeoff is the multi-year exam grind up front before that pay and stability show up.

Yes, 60 percent of live postings are remote, since the core deliverables are models and reports that don't require physical presence. Some employers still want in-office time around quarter-end closes or for client-facing consulting work, so fully remote isn't universal even where it's offered.

The routine calculation work is already partly automated, which is part of why Python and SQL now show up in 40 and 33 percent of postings, but someone still has to choose the assumptions and defend them to a regulator or a board. The job is shifting toward model oversight and judgment rather than manual computation, not disappearing.
